Name: steerability_emergence_pretraining
Title: When Does a Design Lever Get Forged? Tracing the Pretraining Emergence of Causal Feature Steerability in Protein Language Models
Short Hypothesis: In protein language models, the causal STEERABILITY of an interpretable feature (its ability to control the corresponding property in generation) emerges LATER in pretraining than its DECODABILITY (linear readout of the concept), and the emergence time of both is gated by the training-data frequency of the underlying biological concept: rare-but-valid concepts become decodable long before—or without ever—becoming steerable. This decodability-steerability lag is a training-time phenomenon that explains the widely-reported 'decodable-but-inert' anomaly and predicts which design levers a given checkpoint can and cannot provide.
Related Work: Two literatures converge but have never met. (1) Feature-emergence-during-pretraining work is entirely in TEXT LLMs: 'Evolution of Concepts in Language Model Pre-Training' (2025) and 'Crosscoding Through Time' (2025) use crosscoders to track feature formation; 'The Birth of Knowledge' (2025) maps categorical feature emergence across time/space/scale; and most relevantly 'How Does Controllability Emerge in LMs During Pretraining' (2025) shows linear STEERABILITY of text concepts emerges at intermediate stages and varies by concept, linked to linear separability. None studies scientific generative models, none ties emergence to training-DATA-FREQUENCY of the concept, and none contrasts decodability vs causal steerability trajectories for GENERATED scientific objects. (2) Protein-SAE work (InterPLM 2024; ProtSAE 2025; 'From Mechanistic Interpretability to Mechanistic Biology' 2025; automated neuron labelling 2025; motif-gated causal patching 2025) is entirely inference-time on a FINAL checkpoint, and reports the 'decodable-but-inert' anomaly as a static puzzle. Data-scaling/bias work (Scaling and Data Saturation in pLMs 2025; pLMs biased by unequal sequence sampling 2024; Compute-Optimal pLMs 2024) shows data frequency shapes likelihoods but never connects it to feature steerability. We are the first to (i) trace decodability AND causal steerability trajectories across pretraining in a scientific generative model, (ii) test data-frequency as the gating variable via curated rare/common concepts and yearly-snapshot corpora, and (iii) reframe the decodable-but-inert anomaly as a training-time developmental lag with a predictive rule for checkpoint-conditional controllability. This uses Formation Tracing—a genuinely different mechanism strategy from prior inference-time steering studies. Our contribution is two-fold and separable: (a) the PHENOMENON—a decodability-then-steerability developmental lag gated by concept training-frequency; (b) the MEASUREMENT PIPELINE—checkpoint-wise SAE + causal steering + frequency-controlled onset estimation. Null-novelty is well-defined: if the lag is already established in text LMs, the protein-specific frequency-gating and the decodable-but-inert reconciliation remain the delta; if the lag appears in neither text nor protein models, that null itself constrains explanations of the anomaly to non-temporal causes.
Abstract: Interpretability-guided design assumes that if a concept is decodable from a protein language model it can be used as a design lever—yet multiple studies report 'decodable-but-inert' features that read out a concept perfectly but fail to steer generation. We propose that this anomaly is a developmental one: during pretraining, the causal STEERABILITY of a feature emerges strictly later than its DECODABILITY, and both are gated by how frequently the underlying biological concept appears in the training data. We test this by pretraining small ESM-style masked protein LMs (3.5M–35M params, tractable for an academic lab) and saving frequent checkpoints, complemented by publicly available yearly UniRef-snapshot pLMs. At each checkpoint we train a sparse autoencoder and, for a curated bank of concepts spanning a wide data-frequency range (common folds/motifs to rare families and rare property combinations), we measure two trajectories: decodability (probe AUROC of the concept feature) and steerability (causal property change per unit steer in generation, verified by DSSP/ESMFold/HMMER). We hypothesize (i) a consistent decodability-then-steerability ordering with a measurable lag, (ii) that concept training-frequency predicts both onset times, and (iii) that some rare concepts remain decodable-but-inert at convergence—explaining the static anomaly. We further test whether an emergent 'steerability onset' at one scale predicts onset at another, and whether upsampling a rare concept in a controlled retraining accelerates its steerability onset. Results would recast steerability as a trainable, data-dependent developmental property and yield a decision rule for practitioners and scaling researchers: a frequency-and-cheap-checkpoint predictor of which design levers a checkpoint can safely provide—when a decodable concept is usable for control and when it is not.
Experiments:
SHARED SETUP (used by all experiments below). Models: masked protein LMs in the ESM-2 family at three scales, 3.5M, 8M, and 35M parameters, trained from scratch by us on a fixed 20M-sequence random subset of UniRef50 (UniRef50 has ~60M clusters; we use 20M to keep one 8M/35M run inside a single-GPU-week on one A100-40GB). All weights trainable during pretraining; frozen at each checkpoint for probing/steering. Key hyperparameters: masking rate 15%, batch 2048 sequences, max length 256, LR 4e-4 cosine with 2k warmup, AdamW, ~1.0e10 tokens total; we save 18 checkpoints log-spaced in tokens (10^7 ... 10^10). Three pretraining seeds {0,1,2} per scale for the 3.5M and 8M models, one seed for 35M (budget). Independent data-frequency axis: the four public yearly UniRef-snapshot ESM checkpoints where released. SAE: one TopK SAE (k=32, dictionary 8192, trained 100M activations, seed 0) per checkpoint on the mid-layer residual stream (layer at 60% depth), reconstruction FVU reported; a raw-activation linear probe is the SAE-independent decodability control, and a difference-of-means (SAE-free) steering direction is the SAE-independent steerability control. Inter-checkpoint SAE feature-matching (activation-correlation / Hungarian matching across adjacent checkpoints) and per-checkpoint reconstruction FVU are reported so that measured emergence timing reflects feature FORMATION rather than feature reallocation. For every concept we record confound covariates—concept complexity (evaluator/description length), sequence conservation, motif length, Pfam family size, and corpus redundancy—for use in Experiment 2. Concept bank: 40 concepts with hard automated evaluators and exact training-corpus frequency (counted in our 20M subset): 12 common (alpha-helix and beta-sheet fraction via DSSP on ESMFold, GRAVY hydrophobicity, molecular weight, zinc-finger and catalytic-triad motifs via HMMER/PROSITE), 28 deliberately rare (rare Pfam families with 50-500 corpus hits, uncommon motifs, and rare property combinations such as high-beta + high-hydrophilicity). DECODABILITY(concept, checkpoint) = held-out probe AUROC of the best SAE feature (and raw-activation probe) on 2,000 natural sequences. STEERABILITY(concept, checkpoint) = property change per unit steering norm during masked-infilling generation at the largest strength that keeps validity (pseudo-perplexity within 1.5x of unsteered and ESMFold pLDDT >= 0.6*baseline), verified by the concept's own evaluator over 500 generations, with random-direction and unrelated-feature (non-concept) controls subtracted to establish specificity.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- Decodability emerges before steerability: the lag). Tests that within a concept, DECODABILITY crosses its detection threshold at an earlier training-token count than STEERABILITY. Data: the 40-concept bank above, evaluated at all 18 checkpoints x 3 scales. Systems compared, per concept: decodability trajectory vs steerability trajectory across checkpoints. Define onset = first checkpoint at which a trajectory crosses a fixed threshold (decodability AUROC >= 0.75; steerability >= 2x the matched random-direction control effect and property change >= 0.5 SD of the natural-sequence property distribution). Decisive metric: paired difference lag = log10(steerability-onset tokens) - log10(decodability-onset tokens), aggregated over concepts (Wilcoxon signed-rank, Hedges g). Convincing positive: median lag >= 0.3 log10-tokens (i.e. steerability onset at >= 2x the tokens of decodability onset) with signed-rank p < 0.01 in >= 2 of 3 scales. Decision band: median lag in [0.1, 0.3) log10-tokens is INDECISIVE given our 18-checkpoint spacing (a lag below the ~0.13-log10 gap between adjacent checkpoints cannot be resolved); we then densify checkpoints x2 around detected onsets before concluding. Negative result: median lag <= 0 (steerability never later than decodability) refutes the developmental-lag account and is reported as such, constraining explanations of the decodable-but-inert anomaly to non-temporal causes.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- Concept training-frequency gates both onsets, correlational). Tests that higher corpus frequency predicts earlier decodability-onset and steerability-onset, and that steerability-onset is the more frequency-sensitive of the two. Data: the same onsets from Experiment 1 paired with each concept's exact corpus frequency (range 50 to ~2M hits across the 40 concepts). Model: mixed-effects regression of log10(onset tokens) on log10(frequency), random intercept per scale and per concept-family. Decisive metric: standardized slope beta_freq for each onset type and the contrast beta_steer - beta_decode. Convincing positive: beta_freq significantly negative for both (higher frequency -> earlier onset) with steerability strictly more sensitive, |beta_steer| - |beta_decode| >= 0.15 (95% bootstrap CI excludes 0). Decision band: contrast in [0.05, 0.15) means frequency gates onset but the differential sensitivity is UNRESOLVED at n=40 concepts; we report the main frequency effect and flag the contrast as underpowered rather than claim asymmetric gating. Negative: beta_freq CI includes 0 means frequency does not gate onset, sending the causal test (Experiment 3) to adjudicate whether a confound (concept complexity, conservation) drives the null.

Experiment 3 (H2 -- Upsampling a rare concept causally accelerates its steerability-onset). Tests the gating claim causally by manipulating frequency alone. Data/model: retrain the 3.5M model (cheapest, 3 seeds) with 6 chosen rare concepts upsampled 10x versus a matched control run, total tokens held fixed at 1.0e10 so only relative frequency changes. Systems compared: upsampled vs control run, on the 6 treated concepts and 6 untreated rare controls. Decisive metric: shift in steerability-onset (log10 tokens) for treated concepts, upsampled minus control, paired across seeds. Convincing positive: treated concepts advance their steerability-onset by >= 0.3 log10-tokens (95% CI excludes 0) while untreated controls shift by < 0.1 log10-tokens. Decision band: treated advance in [0.1, 0.3) log10-tokens is a WEAK causal effect; we report it as directional support insufficient to claim frequency is the dominant lever. Negative: treated shift indistinguishable from control (< 0.1) means frequency is not the causal gate, overriding any correlational signal from Experiment 2.

Experiment 4 (H3 -- The lag explains decodable-but-inert and predicts a checkpoint's usable levers). Tests that concepts which are decodable-but-inert at convergence are exactly those whose steerability-onset never crosses threshold, and that this is predictable cheaply. Data: convergence checkpoint (10^10 tokens) of all three scales; plus cross-scale onset ordering from all checkpoints. Systems compared: (a) per concept at convergence, decodable-but-inert label (AUROC >= 0.75 AND steerability < threshold) vs the frequency-plus-small-model-onset predictor; (b) steerability-onset ordering at 3.5M vs at 35M. Decisive metrics: (a) fraction of the 40 concepts that are decodable-but-inert at convergence, and AUROC of predicting that label from {log-frequency, 3.5M steerability-onset}; (b) Spearman rho between 3.5M and 35M steerability-onset ranks. Convincing positive: a non-trivial inert fraction (point estimate reported with Wilson CI) with predictor AUROC >= 0.80, and cross-scale rho >= 0.6 (p < 0.01), giving a cheap-model rule for which levers a target checkpoint provides. Decision band: predictor AUROC in [0.65, 0.80) or rho in [0.4, 0.6) means the anomaly is real but only partially predictable; we ship the predictor with its measured error rather than as a guarantee. Negative: inert fraction ~0 (no concept is decodable-but-inert at convergence) means the static anomaly does not reproduce in our models and the explanatory claim is withdrawn; AUROC ~0.5 or rho ~0 means the lag is not predictable and offers no practical lever-forecasting rule.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Small self-trained pLMs may underperform large models, so absolute steerability could be weak; we mitigate by focusing on RELATIVE trajectories/orderings and by cross-checking with public yearly-snapshot pLMs. 2) SAE quality varies across checkpoints and could confound emergence timing; we control with a fixed SAE architecture/hyperparameters per checkpoint, report reconstruction fidelity, and cross-validate decodability with an SAE-independent raw-activation probe. 3) In-silico evaluators (ESMFold, DSSP, HMMER) are proxies for wet-lab truth; claims concern model-internal, training-time controllability, not experimental viability. 4) Frequency-onset correlations could reflect confounds (concept complexity, sequence conservation) rather than raw frequency; the controlled upsampling retraining (Experiment 3) is designed to isolate frequency causally. 5) Checkpoint spacing may miss sharp emergence transitions; we use log-spaced checkpoints and can densify around detected transitions. 6) If decodability and steerability emerge simultaneously (no lag), that is still an informative, publishable result refuting the developmental-lag account and constraining explanations of the decodable-but-inert anomaly. 7) Retraining runs add compute cost but are limited to the smallest models to stay within an academic budget. 8) Concept-bank selection could bias results; the bank is constructed by a pre-registered procedure (fixed evaluators, exact corpus-frequency binning into 12 common / 28 rare concepts, hard automated labels) reported in full so selection bias and reproducibility can be assessed.

Name: hazard_entanglement_asymmetry
Title: Easy to Arm, Hard to Disarm: An Entanglement Asymmetry Between Hazardous and Benign Design Features in Scientific Generative Models
Short Hypothesis: In molecular and protein generative models, interpretable features exhibit a dual-use entanglement asymmetry: hazardous structural properties (toxicophores, known toxin/venom motifs, reactive groups) can be AMPLIFIED cheaply by steering ostensibly-benign, property-labeled features, yet cannot be SUPPRESSED without disproportionate collateral loss of valid, benign design capability. We hypothesize this asymmetry mirrors the capability/safety entanglement documented in text LLMs but is sharper and objectively measurable here because hazard is a verifiable structural fact, and that the degree of asymmetry is predicted by how much a hazard shares its feature subspace with benign design features.
Related Work: SAE-based safety steering is well developed in TEXT LLMs: refusal steering (Steering Language Model Refusal with SAEs, 2024) and detoxification (Breaking Bad Tokens, 2025; GSAE, 2025; Safe-SAIL, 2025) all report that suppressing an unsafe concept degrades general capability, revealing deep entanglement between safety-relevant and general features. Separately, scientific-model interpretability (InterPLM 2024; ProtSAE 2025; pathology-FM SAEs 2024; chemistry-LM SAEs 2025) discovers and steers interpretable features toward single BENIGN target properties, treating hazard only implicitly. The 'Guiding Generative Models for Protein Design' review (2025) notes models undersample rare regions but does not study hazard controllability. No prior work (a) transfers the safety/capability-entanglement phenomenon into SCIENTIFIC generative models where hazard is a structurally-verifiable fact (RDKit SMARTS toxicophores, HMMER toxin motifs) rather than fuzzy text behavior, (b) tests a DIRECTIONAL ASYMMETRY between cheap hazard amplification and costly hazard suppression, or (c) ties that asymmetry to feature-subspace overlap between hazard and benign design. This distinguishes us from my prior 'intervention-leakage' proposal (which asks whether a single-feature suppression leaks through alternative decoding routes) by instead measuring the amplify-vs-suppress cost asymmetry and its collateral impact on legitimate design capability. It converts a known text-LLM tension into an auditable, high-stakes dual-use risk metric for scientific design. We separate the novelty axes explicitly: NEW SETTING (structurally-verifiable hazard oracles replacing fuzzy text behavior) versus NEW MECHANISM (subspace-overlap prediction of the asymmetry). Three testable novelty-bearing claims: (H1) benign, property-labeled knobs cheaply amplify hazard; (H2) suppression is disproportionately costly and damages benign design (the Asymmetry Index, our single PRIMARY endpoint); (H3) hazard/benign feature-subspace overlap predicts and can be orthogonalized to lower that cost—a tested hypothesis, not a post-hoc label. Stakeholders who would act on this: biosecurity auditors (certify whether a steering interface can be safely disarmed), model developers (decide when to expose steering), interpretability researchers, and policy teams.
Abstract: Interpretability-guided design promises controllable scientific generation, but control is dual-use: the same interpretable knobs that add a desired property may also arm a model to produce hazardous objects, and safety measures that suppress hazard may cripple legitimate design. Text-LLM studies report that safety-relevant features are entangled with general capability, so suppressing an unsafe concept degrades benign performance. We ask whether this tension transfers, and sharpens, in scientific generative models where hazard is an objective structural fact. We define hazardous properties with hard, non-model evaluators (toxicophore/PAINS/reactive-group SMARTS in molecules; known toxin/venom/cytolytic motifs in proteins) and benign design properties with cheap oracles (logP, QED, secondary-structure content, foldability). Training sparse autoencoders on a SMILES chemical language model and ESM-2, we test a central phenomenon: an entanglement asymmetry in which hazard is cheaply AMPLIFIED by steering ostensibly-benign, property-labeled features (a small steering budget, high validity), but cannot be SUPPRESSED below baseline without a disproportionate drop in valid benign-design capability. Our PRIMARY endpoint is the Asymmetry Index = (cost to suppress)/(cost to amplify); the Collateral Ratio = benign-design loss per unit hazard removed and the subspace-overlap prediction are secondary. We quantify these comparing single-feature, subspace, and difference-of-means interventions and controlling for the known pitfall that SAE-reconstructed steering vectors are unreliable. We then test whether the asymmetry is predicted by the feature-subspace overlap between each hazard and benign design directions. A clean-disarmament (low-asymmetry) result is equally valuable, reported as a positive safety finding. Results give biosecurity auditors and model developers a measurable dual-use risk profile and a practical audit—when to deploy steering, when to avoid it, how to certify a safety intervention.
Experiments:
SHARED SETUP. Models: a GPT-style SMILES chemical LM (a public ~90M-parameter checkpoint pretrained on ChEMBL/ZINC) and ESM-2 at 150M and 650M parameters. All base weights frozen; only SAEs are trained. SAEs: TopK (k=32) and Matryoshka variants, dictionary 16384, trained on 200M residual-stream activations at a mid layer (60% depth), seeds {0,1}, FVU reported. HAZARD properties, hard non-model evaluators: molecules -- toxicophore/PAINS SMARTS and reactive/electrophilic-group and structural-alert counts via RDKit (10 alert classes); proteins -- known toxin/venom/cytolytic motifs via HMMER against curated toxin HMMs plus regex (8 motif classes). BENIGN design properties, cheap oracles: molecules -- logP band, QED, ring/scaffold target, synthetic accessibility (SA); proteins -- alpha-helix/beta-sheet fraction (DSSP on ESMFold), GRAVY, a fold/foldability target. VALIDITY gates: RDKit-validity + SA<=6 for molecules; ESMFold pLDDT>=0.6 + pseudo-perplexity within 1.5x baseline for proteins. Steering budget = L2 norm of the added intervention vector, in units of the mean residual-stream norm at the site (so "0.5" = half the typical activation norm); all costs reported in these normalized budget units. Every intervention uses SAE decoder directions and difference-of-means directions DIRECTLY (never SAE re-encodings of steering vectors, the documented OOD/sign pitfall), with a norm-matched random-direction control. 18 hazard/motif classes total across domains; 500 generations per condition (a class-level bootstrap over 18 classes gives ~80% power to detect an Asymmetry-Index median >= 3 vs the null of 1 at a per-class SD of ~1.5). BASELINES for every direction-based claim: SAE-decoder directions, difference-of-means, supervised linear-probe directions, random norm-matched subspaces, and native property gradients where differentiable. ABLATIONS reported throughout: SAE layer (40/60/80% depth), SAE type (TopK vs Matryoshka), feature-bank construction (probe-AUROC threshold), and the thresholds defining hazard baseline (occurrence) and hazard removed (<5%). Steering is always applied inside the validity gate so a suppression cost cannot be dismissed as generic degeneracy.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- Benign knobs cheaply amplify hazard). Tests that steering ostensibly-benign, property-labeled features raises hazard occurrence in finished objects at a small budget. Data/systems: for each of the 18 hazard classes, feature bank of benign property-labeled features (identified by probe AUROC>=0.8 on 2,000 held-out natural objects) vs the hazard's own features; compare amplification via benign features, via hazard features, and via norm-matched random directions. Decisive metric: AMPLIFICATION COST = minimal budget to raise hazard occurrence in valid finished objects from baseline to 50%. Convincing positive: median amplification cost via benign features <= 0.5 budget units (and clearly below the random-direction control, which should need >> 1.0 or never reach 50% within validity). Decision band: cost in (0.5, 1.0] units is MODERATE -- hazard is amplifiable but not "cheap"; we report it as amplifiable-with-effort, not cheap arming. Negative: benign features cannot reach 50% hazard within the validity budget at any tested strength (up to 2.0) means benign knobs do not arm the model, refuting H1 for that class.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- Suppression is disproportionately costly: the asymmetry). Tests that driving hazard below baseline costs far more, and damages benign design, than amplification does. Data/systems: same hazard classes; interventions are single-feature, k-dim subspace (SVD of correlated hazard features), and difference-of-means, each compared to a norm-matched random-direction suppression control. Decisive metric (primary): ASYMMETRY INDEX = suppression cost / amplification cost, where suppression cost = minimal budget to drive baseline hazard occurrence below 5% while holding validity. Secondary: COLLATERAL RATIO = benign-design success loss per unit hazard-occurrence removed, benign-design success = hitting a battery of legitimate targets (logP/QED/scaffold; secondary-structure/fold). Convincing positive: median Asymmetry Index >= 3 (suppression >= 3x costlier than amplification) with Collateral Ratio significantly above the random-direction control (95% bootstrap CI over classes excludes 1x). Decision band: Asymmetry Index in [1.5, 3) is a WEAK asymmetry -- reported as present but modest; in [0.67, 1.5) hazard is essentially as cheap to suppress as to amplify (symmetric). Negative: Asymmetry Index <= 0.67 or Collateral Ratio at/below the random control means hazard can be cleanly disarmed -- a valuable positive safety result reported as refuting the asymmetry.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- Objectively measurable and sharper than the text-LLM analogue). Tests that the entanglement here is quantifiable against a structural ground truth and at least as sharp as the reported text-LLM capability/safety degradation. Data/systems: the Collateral Ratio and validity/diversity curves from Experiment 2, benchmarked against a norm-matched random-direction suppression (the text-LLM-style "generic capability degradation" reference) within the same pipeline. Decisive metric: gap between hazard-suppression Collateral Ratio and the random-direction Collateral Ratio at equal hazard removal, plus the fraction of hazard classes whose ratio exceeds the random reference. Convincing positive: hazard-specific suppression shows Collateral Ratio strictly above random in >= 70% of classes (structured, not generic, entanglement) with every quantity computed from hard structural evaluators (0% reliance on a learned hazard model). Decision band: 50-70% of classes above random is PARTIAL -- entanglement is structured for some hazards only; we enumerate which. Negative: <= 50% (hazard suppression no worse than a random norm-matched edit) means the collateral is generic capability loss, not hazard-specific entanglement, and the "sharper here" claim is withdrawn.

Experiment 4 (H4 -- Subspace overlap predicts the asymmetry). Tests that a hazard's feature-subspace overlap with benign design directions predicts its Asymmetry Index and Collateral Ratio, and that orthogonalized suppression lowers collateral. Data/model: for each hazard class compute subspace overlap with benign directions (mean principal-angle cosine / effective shared rank) from the SAE dictionary; regress Asymmetry Index and Collateral Ratio on overlap (Spearman, bootstrap CI over 18 classes). Mitigation arm: subspace suppression projecting out only the hazard-specific complement (orthogonalized against benign directions) vs plain suppression at equal hazard removal. Decisive metric: Spearman rho between overlap and Asymmetry Index; and Collateral-Ratio reduction from orthogonalized vs plain suppression. Convincing positive: rho >= 0.6 (p<0.05) AND orthogonalized suppression cuts Collateral Ratio by >= 30% at matched hazard removal. Decision band: rho in [0.3, 0.6) means overlap is one factor among several -- reported as partial predictor; orthogonalized-suppression gain in [10%, 30%) is a modest mitigation. Negative: rho <= 0.3 means overlap does not predict the asymmetry (the mechanism claim fails, though the phenomenon from Experiments 1-2 may still stand), and no orthogonalization benefit means the collateral is irreducible in feature space.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Hazard and benign properties are defined by in-silico structural evaluators (RDKit SMARTS, HMMER, ESMFold); these are proxies for real-world hazard/function, so claims concern model-internal, structurally-defined dual-use controllability rather than wet-lab harm. We deliberately study only structural-alert-level hazards with unambiguous detectors and avoid synthesizable-threat detail. 2) The asymmetry could depend on steering budget definition; we sweep budgets and report full amplify/suppress curves rather than single points. 3) SAE quality/layer choice may confound which features 'encode' hazard vs benign; we control with multiple SAE variants, probe verification, difference-of-means directions, and random-direction controls, and we avoid the SAE-reconstructed-steering-vector pitfall documented in the literature. 4) Subspace-overlap predictor may be underpowered with few hazard classes; we include many toxicophore/motif classes across both domains. 5) If no asymmetry is found (hazard is as easy to suppress as amplify, with low collateral), that is a valuable, publishable positive safety result establishing that scientific generative models can be cleanly disarmed. 6) We will responsibly report aggregate metrics and mitigations (orthogonalized suppression), not recipes for producing specific hazardous objects.

Name: steering_fails_on_memorized_designs
Title: You Can't Steer a Memory: Interpretable-Feature Control Silently Fails on Memorized Scientific Designs
Short Hypothesis: Scientific generative models occupy a hybrid regime that memorizes some outputs (near-verbatim training retrievals) and generalizes others. We hypothesize that interpretable-feature steering, the dominant paradigm for controllable design, CAUSALLY FAILS on memorized generations while succeeding on generalized ones—because memorized objects sit at contractive attractors whose internal representations are 'spiky' and resist perturbation. Consequently, a cheap, intervention-free representation-spikiness score predicts, before any steering, whether a given generation is controllable, and steering evaluated only on aggregate averages hides a large, systematically uncontrollable memorized subpopulation.
Related Work: Two lines converge here for the first time. (1) Memorization geometry: 'Generalization of Diffusion Models Arises with a Balanced Representation Space' (2025) proves memorized samples yield spiky representations and are NOT steerable while generalized samples are steerable in representation space; 'Overparameterized autoencoders implement associative memory' (2018/2020) shows memorized examples are contractive attractors. (2) Scientific-model controllability: InterPLM (2024), ProtSAE (2025), and chemistry-LM SAE steering demonstrate interpretable features steer protein/molecule generation, but ALWAYS report AGGREGATE property gains and never partition outputs by memorization status. Meanwhile 'Transformer Learning in Sequence-Based Drug Design Depends on Compound Memorization' (2026) and protein-LM data-leakage studies (2024/2025) show scientific generative models are heavily memorization-driven, yet treat this as a benchmark-inflation problem, not a controllability problem. No prior work (a) tests whether the memorized-not-steerable geometry transfers to SCIENTIFIC generative models where memorization is objectively measurable via sequence identity to the training set, (b) shows interpretable-feature steering causally fails on the memorized subpopulation, or (c) validates a pre-flight spikiness score that predicts per-generation controllability. This distinguishes the proposal from all my prior steering-focused ideas (which assumed the target is steerable) and from the memorization literature (which ignores controllable design). Our PRIMARY contribution is a transferable cross-modal PHENOMENON—memorized-not-steerable geometry reappearing in scientific sequence models—plus a new per-generation OPERATIONAL definition of controllability; the intervention-free spikiness predictor is a secondary, practical by-product. This is a new evaluation STANDARD, not merely a mechanistic curiosity: it tells design teams, IP/safety auditors, and controllability researchers to partition steering metrics by memorization status, to pre-flight-filter which generations are controllable, and to audit the memorized subpopulation before trusting an aggregate property gain.
Abstract: Interpretable-feature steering has become the standard tool for controllable design of proteins and molecules, and it is universally evaluated by average property gains across many generations. We ask whether that average conceals a systematic failure mode. Recent geometry work shows generative models occupy a hybrid regime—memorizing some outputs as contractive attractors with 'spiky' internal representations while generalizing others—and that memorized samples resist representation-space steering. Scientific generative models are known to be heavily memorization-driven, and, uniquely, memorization here is objectively measurable: a generation is memorized if it is near-identical to a training sequence. We hypothesize that interpretable-feature steering is systematically far less effective on memorized generations than on generalized ones, so aggregate steering metrics hide a large, poorly-controllable subpopulation, and we quantify how often aggregate benchmarks mislead. Using ESM-style protein language models and a SMILES chemical language model with sparse autoencoders, we label each generation as memorized or generalized via sequence/structure identity to the (known) training corpus, then measure per-generation steerability of feature interventions against cheap property oracles. We test three claims: (1) steering property-gain and validity are far lower on memorized than generalized generations at matched steering budget; (2) an intervention-free representation-spikiness score (activation standard deviation / SAE-feature concentration) predicts per-generation steerability before any intervention, enabling a pre-flight controllability filter; and (3) nudging generation away from memorized attractors (light noise/temperature or a 'de-spiking' repulsion from the nearest training neighbor) restores steerability, at a measurable novelty cost. Results would reveal a hidden, safety- and IP-relevant blind spot, change steering-evaluation protocol (report metrics split by memorization status), and provide a cheap pre-flight test for when steering can be trusted.
Experiments:
SHARED SETUP. Generators with KNOWN training corpora so memorization is objectively measurable: a self-trained ESM-style masked protein LM at 8M and 35M parameters on a defined 10M-sequence UniRef50 subset (one seed each; base weights frozen after training), plus a public ProtGPT2 checkpoint with a documented training set; and a GPT-style SMILES chemical LM (~90M) trained by us on a defined ChEMBL/ZINC subset. SAEs: TopK (k=32, dictionary 16384) and Matryoshka on the mid-layer (60% depth) residual stream, trained on 200M activations, seeds {0,1}, FVU reported. Cheap property oracles: proteins -- alpha-helix/beta-sheet fraction (DSSP on ESMFold), GRAVY, molecular weight, motifs (HMMER/regex); molecules -- RDKit logP, QED, ring/aromatic counts, functional-group SMARTS. Validity gates: ESMFold pLDDT>=0.6 + pseudo-perplexity within 1.5x baseline (proteins); RDKit-validity + SA<=6 (molecules). Feature bank: property-linked SAE features (probe AUROC>=0.8 on 2,000 held-out natural objects) plus difference-of-means directions as a non-SAE baseline. Steering budget in normalized activation-norm units (as in the norm of the added vector / mean site activation norm). Per-generation STEERABILITY = target-property change per unit budget within the validity gate, with norm-matched random-direction control subtracted.

Experiment 1 (H4/H1 -- Memorization labels split a large corpus, and the aggregate average hides the split). Tests that a substantial memorized subpopulation exists and that reporting only the mean steering gain conceals it. Data: 20,000 unsteered generations per model. Labels: MEMORIZED if nearest-training-example identity is high -- proteins: sequence identity >= 90% (mmseqs2/BLAST), optionally TM-score corroborated; molecules: Morgan-fingerprint Tanimoto >= 0.9 or exact canonical-SMILES match; GENERALIZED if nearest identity is low (proteins <= 50%, molecules Tanimoto <= 0.4). Decisive metric: memorized fraction per model (Wilson CI) and its dependence on model size and sampling temperature; plus the bimodality (dip test) of the aggregate per-generation steering-gain distribution. Convincing positive: memorized fraction >= 10% for at least one model AND the aggregate steering-gain distribution is significantly bimodal (dip test p<0.01) once split by label. Decision band: memorized fraction in [3%, 10%) means the blind spot exists but is small -- reported as a minority subpopulation; dip-test p in [0.01, 0.05) is suggestive-only bimodality. Negative: memorized fraction < 3% across all models means no meaningful memorized subpopulation exists here and the aggregate-blind-spot claim (H4) does not apply to these models.

Experiment 2 (H1 -- Steering fails on memorized, succeeds on generalized). Tests the core causal-status contrast at matched budget. Data/systems: memorized vs generalized generations matched on baseline property value and sequence length (to remove confounds); apply feature steering and difference-of-means steering at a swept budget {0.1...1.0}; norm-matched random-direction control. Decisive metric (primary): steerability GAP = generalized minus memorized per-generation steerability, mixed-effects model with memorization status as key factor (effect size, 95% CI), plus the control-validity frontier area per subpopulation. Convincing positive: generalized steerability exceeds memorized by >= 0.5 SD of the per-generation steerability distribution (CI excludes 0) with the same ordering in >= 3 of the 4 models. Decision band: gap in [0.2, 0.5) SD is a REAL but modest effect -- reported as partial, not "causal failure"; the aggregate frontier likely still usable on memorized. Negative: gap <= 0.2 SD (memorized as steerable as generalized) is a clean negative result that the diffusion-model memorized-not-steerable geometry does NOT transfer to these sequence models, and H1 is withdrawn.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- Intervention-free spikiness predicts controllability pre-steer). Tests that a cheap representation-spikiness score forecasts per-generation steerability before any intervention, and does so at least as well as the expensive memorization label. Data: all labeled generations from Experiment 1. Spikiness scores at the intervention site: activation SD across dimensions; SAE-feature concentration (top-feature mass fraction / feature-vector entropy); local contractivity proxy (representation change under small input perturbation). Systems: spikiness vs concept-correlation vs the (expensive) memorization label as predictors of the measured steerability from Experiment 2. Decisive metric: Spearman rho and R^2 of spikiness-vs-steerability, and precision@k for selecting the top-k most steerable generations. Convincing positive: rho >= 0.5 (bootstrap CI excludes 0) AND precision@100 >= 0.8 AND spikiness matches or beats the memorization-label predictor -- a usable intervention-free pre-flight filter with quantified compute saved. Decision band: rho in [0.3, 0.5) or precision@100 in [0.6, 0.8) means spikiness is a weak screen -- reported with its measured error, not as a reliable gate. Negative: rho <= 0.3 means spikiness does not predict steerability and the pre-flight-filter claim fails, even if the H1/H2 phenomenon holds.

Experiment 4 (H2 -- The attractor mechanism: leaving the memorized attractor restores steerability). Tests causally that spikiness/contractive-attractor geometry, not merely the memorization label, is what blocks steering. Data/systems: on memorized generations, apply three de-attractor interventions before steering -- (a) mild temperature/nucleus widening, (b) initial-token/masked-position perturbation, (c) explicit "de-spiking" repulsion from the SAE-representation of the nearest training neighbor -- each vs an untreated memorized control. Decisive metric: steerability gain (post minus pre de-attractor) on memorized generations, paired; reported jointly with the NOVELTY cost (drop in nearest-training-neighbor identity) and validity cost. Convincing positive: de-spiking raises memorized steerability to within 0.2 SD of the generalized baseline (recovering >= 60% of the Experiment-2 gap) at a novelty cost that keeps outputs below the memorized identity threshold. Decision band: gap recovery in [30%, 60%) is partial causal support -- the attractor account is one contributor; recovery achievable only at novelty cost that itself de-memorizes the object is reported as confounded (spikiness and memorization not separable here). Negative: no steerability gain from any de-attractor intervention means the contractive-attractor mechanism is not what blocks steering, so H2 is unsupported even if H1 holds descriptively.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Requires knowing the training corpus to label memorization; we mitigate by self-training small models on defined subsets and using public checkpoints with documented training sets, and by using high-similarity thresholds that give conservative memorized labels. 2) In-silico oracles/validity (ESMFold, RDKit) are proxies for wet-lab function; claims concern model-internal controllability and design reliability, not experimental viability. 3) Lower steerability on memorized generations could be confounded by their baseline property values or length; we control via matched-pair comparison and mixed-effects modeling. 4) Spikiness might merely correlate with memorization rather than causing low steerability; Experiment 4 (de-spiking restores steerability) is the causal test that disentangles this. 5) SAE quality/layer choice could affect both spikiness and steerability; we control with multiple SAE variants, layers, and difference-of-means baselines. 6) The word "causal failure" is reserved for the case where the de-spiking intervention (Experiment 4) cleanly restores steerability; otherwise we report a memorization-status ASSOCIATION, not causation. If steering turns out equally effective on memorized generations, that is still a valuable, publishable negative result establishing that the diffusion-model memorized-not-steerable geometry does NOT transfer to scientific sequence models—constraining theories of memorization geometry across modalities. 7) The de-spiking restoration trades novelty for controllability; we quantify this frontier rather than assume a free lunch.

Name: infeasibility_frustration_features
Title: Confidently Impossible: Do Interpretable Features Reveal When a Scientific Generative Model Is Fulfilling a Physically Infeasible Design Spec?
Short Hypothesis: We define a new problem, INFEASIBILITY DETECTION for scientific design specs, distinct from factuality hallucination: when a multi-constraint specification is physically INFEASIBLE (no valid object can satisfy it), scientific generative models do not refuse or signal failure but confidently emit a plausible-looking object that silently violates exactly one constraint. We hypothesize the model internally represents the over-constraint: a compact set of interpretable sparse-autoencoder 'frustration' features fires specifically under infeasible specs, is causally involved in which constraint gets sacrificed, and yields an early, calibrated infeasibility alarm that output-side confidence signals (perplexity, constraint-satisfaction probability) and a constraint-only heuristic fail to provide. We keep four claims separable -- the objective feasibility labels, the silent-violation behavior, the internal frustration features, and the early alarm -- so each stands or falls on its own.
Related Work: SAE interpretability of scientific models (InterPLM 2024; ProtSAE 2025; Steering PLMs/ASPO 2025; the antibody SAE 2025; ProtoMech 2026; Matryoshka SAEs on ESM2-3B 2025) discovers and steers features toward SATISFIABLE single or multiple properties, always assuming a valid target exists, and evaluates whether the property appears. Hallucination-detection SAE work in text/vision LMs (SSL 2025; 'Do I Know This Entity?' 2024) shows features can flag when a model lacks knowledge, but concerns fuzzy factuality, not physically-verifiable constraint infeasibility. Constraint-based design/steering (compositional steering; conditioned generation) presumes feasibility and reports average satisfaction, never asking what happens when the requested constraint set is CONTRADICTORY. No prior work (a) constructs graded feasible-vs-infeasible design specs for proteins/molecules with objective, physics-based feasibility labels, (b) shows models silently and confidently violate constraints under infeasible specs, or (c) identifies interpretable 'frustration/infeasibility' features that fire selectively and act as a calibrated early alarm. This reframes interpretability from a controllability tool into an epistemic-honesty/safety instrument for design, distinct from all my prior steering-focused proposals and from hallucination work in non-scientific domains. DELTA AT A GLANCE. vs hallucination-detection SAEs (SSL 2025; 'Do I Know This Entity?' 2024): they flag fuzzy factual uncertainty, whereas we flag physically-verifiable, over-constrained INFEASIBILITY with objective labels. vs constrained-generation/steering (compositional/conditioned design): they assume a feasible target and report average satisfaction, whereas we study what happens when the constraint set is CONTRADICTORY. Four separable novel contributions: (a) objective feasibility labels, (b) the silent-violation behavior, (c) interpretable frustration features, (d) the early calibrated alarm -- each evaluated independently so the failure of one does not sink the others.
Abstract: Scientific design increasingly means asking a generative model to satisfy several hard constraints at once, yet some constraint combinations are physically infeasible -- no valid protein or molecule can meet them (a compact fold with extreme surface-exposed hydrophobicity; a small molecule combining mutually exclusive substructure and property demands). We define a new problem, infeasibility detection for scientific design specs, and surface a safety-relevant behavior: rather than refusing, models confidently emit a fluent, plausible object that silently violates one constraint, and standard output-side confidence does not flag it. We then ask whether the model internally represents the infeasibility. Using ESM-2 protein language models and a SMILES chemical language model with sparse autoencoders (SAEs), we build formal feasibility ladders -- specs graded from clearly satisfiable to provably infeasible, with objective labels triangulated from three model-independent signals (natural co-occurrence support, structural-incompatibility rules, and long-budget oracle-search failure) and feasibility defined operationally and separately from mere rarity. We report four separable results: (1) the labeled ladders themselves; (2) the silent-violation behavior and the blindness of output-side confidence; (3) a compact set of interpretable 'frustration' features that fire specifically under infeasible specs, controlling for constraint identity, and are causally involved in which constraint is sacrificed; and (4) an early, calibrated mid-generation infeasibility alarm that beats perplexity, a constraint-satisfaction probe, and a constraint-only heuristic. A positive alarm supports a concrete workflow -- abort generation, reroute to constraint relaxation/repair, or flag the spec for human revision -- saving downstream synthesis and folding/validation compute. Adopters include design pipelines, active-learning and uncertainty-estimation groups, and safety auditors.
Experiments:
SHARED SETUP. Models: ESM-2 at 150M and 650M parameters and a GPT-style SMILES chemical LM (~90M), all base weights frozen. SAEs: TopK (k=32, dictionary 16384) and Matryoshka on the mid-layer (60% depth) residual stream, trained on 200M activations, seeds {0,1}, FVU reported. Constraint evaluators (hard, non-model): proteins -- secondary-structure fraction (DSSP on ESMFold), GRAVY, net charge, molecular weight, motif presence (HMMER/regex); molecules -- RDKit logP, QED, ring/aromatic counts, functional-group SMARTS, molecular weight. Validity gates: ESMFold pLDDT>=0.6 + pseudo-perplexity within 1.5x baseline (proteins); RDKit-validity + SA<=6 (molecules). FEASIBILITY LADDERS: for 24 constraint pairs/triples per domain, a graded ladder from clearly feasible to provably infeasible, with objective labels triangulated from three model-independent signals -- (a) empirical joint co-occurrence support over a 1M-object natural corpus (spec outside joint support = candidate-infeasible), (b) SMARTS/structure-incompatibility rules (mutually exclusive substructures; protein structure-property conflicts such as >80% beta-sheet AND high solvent-exposed hydrophobicity), (c) an oracle-search control -- a genetic optimizer over sequences/molecules with a large fixed budget whose persistent failure corroborates infeasibility. Core claims are restricted to ladder rungs where all three signals agree; label confidence reported per rung. To validate the labels we add STRESS TESTS where oracle-search is known to fail for reasons OTHER than infeasibility (deceptive but satisfiable specs with tiny feasible basins; rugged-but-feasible landscapes); rungs where oracle-failure is not corroborated by signals (a)/(b) are excluded from infeasible labels. SAE frustration features are selected on a TRAIN set of constraint families, and all reported discrimination/alarm numbers are computed on HELD-OUT constraint families and spec instances to preclude leakage. Constraint steering uses property-feature and difference-of-means directions.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- Silent violation under infeasible specs, and output-side confidence is blind). Tests that as feasibility drops, models emit valid, fluent objects that violate exactly one constraint rather than refusing, and that output-side confidence does not track feasibility. Data/systems: steer generation toward each spec across all ladder rungs, 500 generations per rung; compare behavior across the feasibility gradient. Decisive metric (primary): SILENT-VIOLATION RATE = fraction of infeasible-spec generations that remain valid/fluent but violate exactly one constraint (vs refusing/degenerating), with the sacrificed-constraint identity tallied for systematicity; secondary: discrimination (AUROC) of output-side confidence (pseudo-perplexity, generation likelihood, a constraint-satisfaction probe) for true feasibility. Convincing positive: silent-violation rate >= 60% on all-signals-agree infeasible rungs AND output-side-confidence AUROC in [0.45, 0.60] (near chance). Decision band: silent-violation rate in [40%, 60%) means the behavior is common but not dominant -- reported as such; output-side AUROC in (0.60, 0.70] means output confidence is a weak-but-nonzero feasibility signal, tempering the "fail to provide" claim. Negative: silent-violation rate < 40% (models often refuse/degenerate) OR output-side AUROC > 0.70 (output confidence already flags infeasibility) refutes H1's framing and removes the need for an internal alarm.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- A compact set of frustration features fires specifically under infeasible specs). Tests that identifiable SAE features discriminate infeasible-vs-feasible specs while controlling for constraint identity (so they detect CONFLICT, not one property). Data: SAE features scored at multiple generation-progress fractions across the ladders. Systems: per-feature discrimination of infeasible-vs-feasible, computed WITHIN matched constraint identity, vs the best single-property feature as a baseline. Decisive metric: AUROC (and mutual information) of the top-m frustration-feature set for infeasibility, and its sparsity (how many features reach AUROC>=0.75). Convincing positive: a compact set (<= 20 features) reaches AUROC >= 0.80 for infeasibility while single-property-feature baselines stay <= 0.65 -- i.e. the signal is conflict-specific, not property-specific. Decision band: top-set AUROC in [0.65, 0.80) means partial internal representation of infeasibility -- reported as weak evidence; if the property-feature baseline also reaches >= 0.65 the features may track a single property, flagged as unresolved. Negative: no feature set exceeds AUROC 0.65 for infeasibility beyond the property baseline means the model does not compactly represent over-constraint, refuting H2.

Experiment 3 (H2 -- Frustration features are causal for conflict resolution). Tests that intervening on the frustration features changes the model's silent-violation behavior specifically. Data/systems: ablate the frustration-feature set and, separately, amplify it, vs random-direction and matched-single-property-feature controls, on infeasible-spec generations. Decisive metric: change in which constraint is sacrificed (shift rate) and in violation magnitude under ablation; change toward hedging/lower-confidence completions under amplification. Convincing positive: ablation shifts the sacrificed-constraint distribution or violation magnitude by an effect size >= 0.5 SD beyond both controls (CI excludes controls), establishing specificity. Decision band: effect in [0.2, 0.5) SD above controls is weak causal support -- reported as correlational-leaning. Negative: intervention indistinguishable from controls means the features are not causal for conflict resolution and the "model knows" claim reduces to a decodable correlate, reported honestly.

Experiment 4 (H3 -- Early, calibrated infeasibility alarm beating output-side signals). Tests that the frustration-feature score read off mid-generation gives an earlier and better-calibrated infeasibility alarm than output-side confidence and a black-box probe. Data/systems: deploy the frustration-feature score at generation-progress fractions {0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0}; baselines -- partial perplexity/likelihood, a constraint-satisfaction probe on the partial object, a CONSTRAINT-ONLY HEURISTIC that predicts infeasibility from the requested constraint values alone (no model internals), and a black-box raw-activation probe. Decisive metric (primary): forecast AUROC for infeasibility vs generation progress, plus calibration ECE; secondary: earliest progress fraction at which AUROC>=0.80 (earliest-reliable-detection) and precision@k for flagging infeasible specs. Convincing positive: the frustration-feature alarm reaches AUROC>=0.80 by 50% progress with ECE<=0.10, beating output-side baselines by >= 0.10 AUROC at that progress point, with quantified compute saved by aborting infeasible requests before full generation + ESMFold/validation. Decision band: alarm AUROC in [0.70, 0.80) at 50% progress, or advantage over the black-box probe in [0.03, 0.10) AUROC, means the internal alarm works but its edge over cheaper signals is marginal -- reported with the interpretability/localization payoff as the differentiator. Negative: the frustration-feature alarm does not beat partial-perplexity/constraint-probe baselines (advantage <= 0.03 AUROC) means output-side signals suffice and the internal-alarm contribution collapses to interpretation only.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Feasibility labels are the crux and are imperfect: empirical co-occurrence support, SMARTS/structure incompatibility rules, and oracle-search failure are all in-silico proxies for true physical infeasibility. We mitigate by triangulating three independent signals and restricting core claims to specs where all three agree, and by reporting label-confidence-stratified results. 2) 'Infeasible' vs merely 'rare/hard' is a continuum; the oracle-search control and graded ladder are designed to separate genuinely impossible from hard-but-possible, but boundary cases will be noisy—reported explicitly. 3) In-silico validity/property evaluators (ESMFold, RDKit) are proxies for wet-lab truth; claims concern model-internal epistemic signals, not experimental viability. 4) Frustration features might merely track the individual conflicting properties rather than their conflict; the constraint-identity control in feature selection and the causal conflict-resolution test are designed to rule this out. 5) The internal alarm may not beat a black-box raw-activation probe on raw AUROC; even so, interpretability (localizing the conflict), calibration, and early detection are the contribution and are reported honestly. 6) If models turn out to reliably signal infeasibility via output confidence, that is still a valuable positive result about epistemic honesty in scientific generative models. 7) SAE quality/layer choice could confound; controlled via multiple SAE variants, layers, and difference-of-means baselines. 8) Negative-result reading: if a constraint-only heuristic or output-side confidence already predicts infeasibility well, the internal-alarm contribution is withdrawn and we report that practitioners can rely on those cheaper checks; if none suffices, the result establishes that explicit feasibility checking remains necessary before synthesis/validation.

Name: steering_reliability_collapse
Title: Controlled but Unrepresentable: Does Interpretable-Feature Steering Push Scientific Generative Models Into Their Own Confidence Blind Spots?
Short Hypothesis: Interpretable-feature steering is judged almost entirely by whether a target-property predictor improves. We hypothesize a distinct, currently-unmeasured failure: steering an interpretable feature to control a property silently drags generation into regions where the model's OWN representation becomes unreliable (its embedding drifts toward random-like, low-information vectors), because steering displaces activations off the training manifold along directions the feature was never calibrated for -- so the apparent property gain is least trustworthy exactly where steering is strongest, even when the finished object is valid and satisfies the predictor. We further hypothesize that a cheap, intervention-free, pre-registered representation-reliability score declines monotonically with steering strength beyond what a matched-OOD-but-unsteered control explains, predicts per-generation whether the claimed property is real versus illusory, and can gate steering to keep only trustworthy designs -- an axis existing property-predictor-plus-validity evaluation misses.
Related Work: Two threads meet for the first time. (1) SAE/neuron steering of scientific generative models (InterPLM 2024; ProtSAE 2025; FoldSAE 2025; Automated Neuron Labelling 2025; Steering PLMs/ASPO 2025; ProtoMech 2026; antibody SAE 2025) all report property GAIN from steering and evaluate success via property predictors; none asks whether steering pushes outputs into regions where the model can no longer reliably represent them. (2) Representation-reliability work—'Quantifying Uncertainty in Protein Representations Across Models and Tasks' (2025) shows pLM embeddings for undersampled sequences become vector-indistinguishable from random, and 'Quantifying Feature Space Universality' plus data-saturation studies show embedding quality tracks training coverage—but this is studied only for NATURAL inputs, never as a CONSEQUENCE of steering, and never linked to the trustworthiness of controlled designs. No prior work (a) shows steering induces representation-reliability collapse, (b) demonstrates that property predictors and validity checks fail to detect this while an internal reliability score does, or (c) uses reliability to gate steering. This is distinct from my prior proposals on memorization-attractors (about contractive attractors resisting steering), validity-foresight (about invalid finished objects), and infeasible-spec frustration (about contradictory constraints): here the finished object can be perfectly valid and hit the property predictor, yet sit in a representational blind spot that makes the control claim untrustworthy. DELTA. The reliability/OOD literature ('Quantifying Uncertainty in Protein Representations' 2025) studies degraded embeddings for naturally undersampled inputs; our contribution is that STEERING actively INDUCES this collapse and ties it to the trustworthiness of controlled designs -- a steering-induced, not input-given, effect, separated from generic distribution shift by a matched-OOD-but-unsteered control. Primary novelty is the phenomenon; the pre-registered reliability score and the gating controller are secondary.
Abstract: Interpretable-feature steering is the dominant tool for controllable design of proteins and molecules, and it is judged almost entirely by whether a target-property predictor says the property increased. Our single novel claim is a phenomenon: steering causes the model's representation reliability to collapse in otherwise-valid outputs. The act of steering pushes generation into regions where the model's own embedding becomes unreliable -- drifting toward random-like, low-information vectors -- so the property 'gain' is measured on objects the model can no longer faithfully represent. Because such objects still fold, still parse, and still satisfy an external predictor, standard evaluation misses this. We hypothesize this arises because steering displaces activations off the training manifold; to separate a genuine steering effect from ordinary distribution shift we compare against matched-OOD-but-unsteered sequences. We pre-register a representation-reliability score with three components (distance-to-random, perturbation self-consistency, SAE-feature coherence) and test that it (1) declines monotonically with steering strength beyond the matched-OOD control; (2) predicts per-generation whether a property gain is real (agrees with an independent oracle) versus illusory; (3) beats output-side validity and predictor-confidence at flagging untrustworthy control, with thresholds fixed on a held-out set; and (4) gates steering to recover a trustworthy control-validity-reliability frontier. The result adds representational reliability as a missing evaluation axis: after this work, reporting steering success from property-predictor gain and validity alone is insufficient. The axis is relevant to any controlled generative-science workflow and would be adopted first by binder and molecule design teams shipping steered candidates to expensive validation.
Experiments:
SHARED SETUP. Models: ESM-2 at 150M and 650M parameters and a GPT-style SMILES chemical LM (~90M), base weights frozen. SAEs: TopK (k=32, dictionary 16384) and Matryoshka on the mid-layer (60% depth) residual stream, trained on 200M activations, seeds {0,1}, FVU reported. Feature bank of 20-40 property-linked features (probe AUROC>=0.8 on 2,000 held-out natural objects): proteins -- alpha-helix/beta-sheet fraction, GRAVY, molecular weight, a thermostability proxy head, motifs; molecules -- logP, QED, ring/aromatic counts, functional groups. Property predictors used the way the steering literature uses them (DSSP/ESMFold, biopython, fine-tuned heads, RDKit/SMARTS). Validity gates: ESMFold pLDDT>=0.6 + pseudo-perplexity within 1.5x baseline (proteins); RDKit-validity + SA<=6 (molecules). Steering budget in normalized activation-norm units; SAE-feature, difference-of-means, and norm-matched random-direction interventions. REPRESENTATION-RELIABILITY SCORE (intervention-free), combining: (a) distance-to-random -- Mahalanobis/cosine gap between the object's embedding and the distribution of embeddings of shuffled/random sequences; (b) embedding self-consistency under small input perturbations (masking/dropout); (c) SAE-feature coherence (co-firing consistency vs natural objects); validated on natural held-out objects to track known coverage/neighbor-density signals before any steering use; each component (distance-to-random, perturbation stability, SAE-coherence) is reported individually as an ablation as well as combined, and both the combination weights and the reliability-gate threshold are fixed on a held-out calibration set only, never on test.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- Steering pushes representations toward unreliable regions; H2 -- monotone collapse with strength). Tests that the reliability score declines monotonically with steering strength, often before validity or property-predictor gain break down. Data/systems: for each feature/property, sweep steering strength {0...1.0 budget units}; at each level generate 500 objects and record property-predictor gain, validity, and reliability score; compare SAE-feature, difference-of-means, and random-direction steering, and -- critically -- a MATCHED-OOD-BUT-UNSTEERED control (natural sequences sampled to match the off-manifold distance induced by steering, with no intervention) so a reliability drop attributable to steering can be separated from generic distribution shift. Decisive metric (primary): slope of reliability vs steering strength (mixed-effects), and the COLLAPSE-BEFORE-VALIDITY GAP = steering strength at which reliability crosses the natural-object 5th-percentile threshold minus the strength at which validity fails. Convincing positive: reliability slope significantly negative and monotone (Spearman rho <= -0.7 vs strength) with a positive collapse-before-validity gap >= 0.2 budget units in the majority of properties, and a steering-induced reliability drop exceeding the matched-OOD-but-unsteered control by >= 0.2 SD (isolating steering from generic distribution shift). Decision band: gap in [0, 0.2) budget units means reliability and validity collapse together -- the phenomenon exists but offers little early-warning headroom; reported as such. Negative: non-monotone or flat reliability (rho > -0.3), or a negative gap (validity fails first), refutes H1/H2 -- reliability collapse is not a distinct pre-validity failure mode, a clean negative result.

Experiment 2 (H3 -- Low reliability marks illusory property gains). Tests that the property "gain" is real when reliability is high and illusory when low, adjudicated by an independent oracle. Data/systems: for a subset of steered generations, score the target property with an INDEPENDENT oracle not used in steering (proteins: FoldX/Rosetta-style stability or a distinct structure metric; molecules: a second empirical logP model or docking); stratify by reliability quartile. Decisive metric (primary): predictor-vs-oracle agreement on the target property per reliability quartile (correlation or concordance). Convincing positive: agreement in the top reliability quartile exceeds the bottom quartile by >= 0.3 (correlation units), CI excludes 0 -- gains are trustworthy only when reliable. Decision band: quartile gap in [0.1, 0.3) means reliability weakly tracks trustworthiness -- reported as a soft signal, not a gate. Negative: gap <= 0.1 (predictor-oracle agreement independent of reliability) means the reliability score does not distinguish real from illusory gains, refuting H3 even if collapse (H1/H2) occurs.

Experiment 3 (H4 -- Output-side signals miss it; the internal score catches it). Tests that validity and property-predictor confidence are near-chance at flagging untrustworthy control while the internal reliability score succeeds. Data/systems: predict "low predictor-oracle agreement" (from Experiment 2) using the internal reliability score vs output-side baselines -- the predictor's own confidence, pseudo-perplexity, ESMFold pLDDT / RDKit-validity, and a black-box raw-activation reliability probe. Decisive metric: AUROC and calibration ECE for flagging untrustworthy generations. Convincing positive: reliability-score AUROC >= 0.80 with ECE<=0.10 while output-side validity/property-confidence stay in [0.45, 0.60] (near chance), the SAE score adding which-features-decohere interpretability. Decision band: reliability-score AUROC in [0.65, 0.80), or its edge over the black-box probe in [0.03, 0.10) AUROC, means the internal signal works but its advantage over cheaper signals is marginal -- the interpretability payoff is then the contribution. Negative: output-side signals already reach AUROC>=0.70, or the reliability score fails to beat them, means H4's "completely miss" claim is refuted.

Experiment 4 (H4 -- Reliability-gated steering keeps only trustworthy designs). Tests that gating steering by the reliability score yields a better trustworthy-yield-per-compute frontier than ungated or validity-only gating. Data/systems: a controller that rejects/down-weights steering driving reliability below the natural-object threshold, vs ungated steering and validity-only gating, over the same property battery. Decisive metric (primary): fraction of generations simultaneously oracle-property-satisfying, valid, and reliable (trustworthy yield), and trustworthy-yield-per-unit-compute; secondary: diversity/novelty retention and compute saved by not validating untrustworthy designs. Convincing positive: reliability-gating raises trustworthy yield by >= 20% relative to validity-only gating at equal or lower compute, without collapsing diversity (novelty retained within 10% of ungated). Decision band: improvement in [5%, 20%) is a modest, reported gain; improvement that comes only with a large diversity loss (>10%) is reported as a trade, not a free lunch. Negative: reliability-gating gives <= 5% trustworthy-yield improvement over validity-only gating, meaning the reliability axis adds no practical control value beyond existing checks.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The independent oracle (FoldX/Rosetta/second logP model/docking) is itself an in-silico proxy; the trustworthiness claim rests on DISAGREEMENT between two independent in-silico signals stratified by reliability, not wet-lab truth—stated explicitly. 2) The reliability score could merely correlate with off-distribution-ness rather than causing untrustworthy property claims; we mitigate by (a) validating it on natural objects with known coverage and (b) the reliability-stratified oracle test that ties low reliability to predictor failure, and by random-direction controls. 3) An internal SAE-based reliability score might not beat a black-box raw-activation probe on raw AUROC; even so, interpretability (naming which features decohere) and the frontier/compute gains are the contribution and are reported honestly. 4) Reliability collapse might be trivially entangled with validity collapse; the core test specifically isolates the regime where objects remain valid and predictor-satisfying yet unreliable, and reports the gap—if no such gap exists, that is itself a clean, publishable negative result. 5) SAE quality/layer choice could confound both steering and reliability; controlled via multiple SAE variants, layers, and difference-of-means baselines. 6) In-silico property/validity evaluators are proxies; claims concern model-internal representational trustworthiness of controlled designs, not experimental function. 7) Generalization: we report whether a single reliability threshold and controller transfer across properties, model sizes, and the two modalities, rather than assuming universality; a threshold that must be re-fit per setting is reported as such.

Name: provenance_shortcut_steering
Title: Designing the Database, Not the Molecule: Do Interpretable Features Reveal That Steered Scientific Generators Chase Dataset Provenance Instead of Physics?
Short Hypothesis: When we steer a protein/molecule generative model toward a desired PHYSICAL property (e.g., high thermostability), the model frequently satisfies the target by moving along interpretable features that encode DATASET PROVENANCE (source organism, protein family, structural-database membership, assay batch) rather than the underlying physics. The apparent property gain is a shortcut: it reproduces the provenance signature correlated with the property in the training data, and interpretable features expose this so we can detect it and steer against it.
Related Work: Prior pLM-SAE work (InterPLM 2024; ProtSAE 2025; 'From Mechanistic Interpretability to Mechanistic Biology' 2025; functional-annotation SAE work 2025) repeatedly finds that pLMs represent proteins via a mix of generic biophysical features AND strong 'family-specific'/organism-specific features, and steering studies add a target property by moving along whatever feature correlates with it. Separately, data-leakage and batch-effect work ('Beware of Data Leakage from Protein LLM Pretraining' 2024; thermostability leakage; batch-effect correction literature) shows downstream property predictors are inflated by provenance confounds. Recent critical work ('Dead Salmons of AI Interpretability' 2025; 'Automated Interpretability Metrics Do Not Distinguish Trained and Random Transformers' 2025; single-cell FM interpretability 2026 finding attention captures co-expression not causal signal) warns that interpretable-looking signals may be spurious. NO prior work connects these: no one asks whether interpretable-feature STEERING for design achieves property gains by exploiting provenance-artifact features rather than causal physics, quantifies how often this happens, or uses interpretability to disentangle a provenance-shortcut direction from a physics direction. This is distinct from all my prior proposals (compositionality, off-mode reach, steerability prediction, leakage, reliability collapse), which all assumed the property gain, when achieved, is legitimate. EXPLICIT NOVELTY CLAIMS: (1) generation-time provenance shortcuting (a GENERATOR shifts provenance to hit a property), distinct from prior leakage work on inflated PREDICTORS; (2) interpretability-mediated ATTRIBUTION of the shortcut to specific feature directions; (3) a provenance-shortcut score predicting design degeneration; (4) provenance-invariant steering as a fix, validated by a planted-shortcut positive control. Closest baselines by name: standard feature steering, random-direction steering, supervised provenance classifiers, projection/adversarial debiasing, and leakage-aware evaluation. Affected communities: protein design, molecular generation, interpretability, and ML-for-science benchmarking; the audit is intended as a reporting checklist.
Abstract: Steering interpretable features is the standard way to make protein and molecule generators produce a desired physical property, with success judged by a property predictor. We surface a generation-time phenomenon distinct from known dataset-leakage effects (which concern inflated PREDICTORS): a GENERATOR can satisfy a physical-property target by shifting the DATASET PROVENANCE of its output -- source organism, protein family, structural-database subset, or assay batch that co-occurs with the property in training -- rather than its physics, and interpretability lets us attribute the shortcut to specific feature directions. Training sparse autoencoders on ESM-2 and a SMILES chemical LM, we operationally separate physics-aligned directions (property correlation surviving provenance stratification) from provenance-aligned directions (high mutual information with provenance labels), predefining properties where family is plausibly causal versus clearly non-causal so the shortcut is isolable. We test three claims with pre-registered decision rules: (1) standard steering moves substantially along provenance features (a provenance-subspace displacement fraction), and its gain shrinks under a provenance-controlled oracle (a spurious-gain metric); (2) a per-generation provenance-shortcut score predicts a designer-relevant failure -- outputs collapse onto one provenance group and lose novelty, a wasted-screening cost; and (3) orthogonalizing the steering direction against provenance features preserves genuine, controlled-oracle gain while restoring novelty, validated by a synthetic planted-shortcut positive control. Baselines include standard and random-direction steering, supervised provenance classifiers, and projection-based debiasing. We deliver a provenance-shortcut audit -- usable as a reporting checklist for protein-design, molecular-generation, interpretability, and ML-for-science benchmarking -- that separates designing-the-molecule from designing-the-database. The primary high-stakes setting is protein thermostability, where a provenance shortcut wastes expensive stability screening.
Experiments:
SHARED SETUP. Models: ESM-2 at 150M and 650M parameters (proteins) and a GPT-style SMILES chemical LM (~90M), base weights frozen. SAEs: TopK (k=32, dictionary 16384) and Matryoshka on the mid-layer (60% depth) residual stream, trained on 200M activations, seeds {0,1}, FVU reported. Target PHYSICAL properties with cheap evaluators: proteins -- thermostability proxy (fine-tuned head), GRAVY, secondary-structure fraction (DSSP on ESMFold); molecules -- logP, a solubility proxy, QED. PROVENANCE labels per training object: proteins -- source organism/taxon, Pfam family, PDB/CATH structural-database membership; molecules -- source assay/dataset (ChEMBL target/document id), scaffold class. Validity gates: ESMFold pLDDT>=0.6 + pseudo-perplexity within 1.5x baseline (proteins); RDKit-validity + SA<=6 (molecules). Steering budget in normalized activation-norm units; SAE-feature, difference-of-means, and norm-matched random-direction interventions. ~8 property x domain settings; 500 generations per condition. FEASIBILITY/DATA: SAEs trained on ~200M activations (~1-2 GPU-days each on one A100); provenance metadata coverage -- proteins: organism/taxon and Pfam family for >95% of training objects, PDB/CATH membership for the structured subset; molecules: ChEMBL assay/document id and Bemis-Murcko scaffold for the full training set. We PREDEFINE, per property, whether provenance is plausibly CAUSAL (e.g., family-defining catalytic motifs) or clearly NON-CAUSAL-but-correlated (e.g., thermostability co-occurring with thermophile source), and analyze the two groups separately; the primary high-stakes property is protein thermostability. Layer (60% depth) and dictionary size (16384) are fixed a priori, with robustness to both reported as an ablation. A feature is called provenance-aligned only by a pre-registered rule (provenance mutual information above, and provenance-stratified property partial-correlation below, fixed thresholds) to avoid post hoc labeling.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- Features split into physics-aligned vs provenance-aligned, and standard steering rides provenance). Tests that standard property steering moves substantially along provenance-encoding features. Data: per SAE feature compute correlation with the target property and mutual information with provenance labels over 2,000 held-out natural objects; partition into provenance-aligned (high provenance MI), physics-aligned (property correlation surviving provenance stratification / partial correlation), and mixed. Systems compared: standard steering via best-property-correlated SAE feature and difference-of-means direction vs a norm-matched random direction; decompose the steering displacement onto provenance vs physics feature subspaces. Decisive metric (primary): PROVENANCE-SUBSPACE DISPLACEMENT FRACTION = share of the steering displacement lying in the provenance subspace. Convincing positive: displacement fraction >= 0.4 (median over settings) and clearly above the random-direction control's incidental overlap. Decision band: fraction in [0.2, 0.4) means steering partially rides provenance -- reported as a contributing, not dominant, shortcut. Negative: fraction < 0.2 (steering stays in the physics subspace) refutes H1 for that property -- a valuable positive result that steering targets physics, not database artifacts.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- The gain is spurious: it shrinks under a provenance-controlled oracle). Tests that the property gain scored by a provenance-decorrelated oracle is much smaller than by the naive predictor.
